final.memo:
Charlie and I have looked at the offering for this social network, but we find the business falls outside our circle of competence [D01]. While the company has achieved rapid user growth, it lacks the long, consistent record of returns on capital that we require before committing Berkshire's capital [D01], [D02].

We are particularly concerned by the competitive landscape, where entrenched players like Google contest the advertising dollars the company seeks to capture [D06]. Furthermore, the dual-class voting structure places absolute control in the hands of one individual, leaving minority shareholders without any meaningful oversight of capital allocation [D01], [D05].

Most importantly, the price being asked today is disconnected from the business's current earning power [D02]. At a valuation of $104 billion and an implied P/E of 104x, the initial earnings yield is a mere 0.96% [D02]. This offers no margin of safety for the investor, particularly when net income has recently shown signs of decline [D01], [D02].

Investing in this company would be akin to betting on a race where the horse has never run a full mile, at a price that assumes it will win every race for the next decade. We prefer to hold cash or invest in businesses we can understand and value with confidence [D08].
